metadata.title: Indopco, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79 (1992) (No. 90-1278)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Indopco, Inc. v. Commissioner

Opinion filed: 1992-02-26

Docket No.: 90-1278

Citations:
• 117 L. Ed. 2d 226
• 112 S. Ct. 1039
• 503 U.S. 79
• 1992 U.S. LEXIS 1374

Case holding summaries:
• stating that deductions are strictly a matter of legislative grace, and taxpayers bear the burden of proving that they are entitled to claim the deduction
• Justice Blackmun once again writing for the Court
• holding that "where no specific asset or useful life can be ascertained, * * * [a capital expenditure] is deducted upon the dissolution of the enterprise."
• explaining that deductions are a matter of legislative grace
• deductions are "strictly construed and allowed only as there is a clear provision therefore"
• stating that deductions are strictly a matter of legislative grace, and taxpayers bear the burden of proving that they are entitled to any claimed deduction
• noting the “familiar rule” that income tax deductions are “a matter of legislative grace”
• explaining that “deductions are strictly construed and allowed only ‘as there is a clear provision thereof’” (quoting New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, 292 U.S. 435, 440 (1934))
• "while business expenditures are currently deductible, a capital expenditure usually is amortized and depreciated over the life of the relevant asset ..."
• holding that an expenditure that produces a significant future benefit is a capital expenditure under section 263(a)
• “[T]his Court has noted the familiar rule that an income tax deduction is a matter of legislative grace and that the burden of clearly showing the right to the claimed deduction is on the taxpayer.” (internal cita- tions and quotations omitted)
• "'[A]n income tax deduction is a matter of legislative grace and * * * the burden of clearly showing the right to the claimed deduction is on the taxpayer[.]'"
• requiring capitalization where the expenditure produces a significant future benefit
• stating generally that "the Code endeavors to match expenses with the revenues of the taxable period to which they are properly attributable, thereby resulting in a more accurate calculation of net income for tax purposes"
• “[T]he burden of clearly showing the right to the claimed deduction is on the taxpayer.”
• holding that income tax deductions are a matter of legislative grace and are to be narrowly construed
• “[D]eductions are exceptions to the norm of capitalization . . . .”
• identifying benefits of transformation from public to private company, such as avoidance of shareholder-relations expenses and administrative advantages of reducing the number of classes and shares of outstanding stock
• capitalization generally required to match an expense with the income to be generated therefrom
• stating that deductions are strictly a matter of legislative grace, and taxpayers bear the burden of proving that they are entitled to claim the deduction
• observing that “an income tax deduction is a matter of legislative grace and that the burden of clearly showing the right to the claimed deduction is on the taxpayer” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• stating that deductions are strictly a matter of legislative grace and taxpayers bear the burden of proving that they are entitled to claim the deduction
• identifying benefits of transformation from public to private company, such as avoidance of shareholder-relations expenses and administrative advantages of reducing the number of classes and shares of outstanding stock
• capitalization generally required to match an expense with the income to be generated therefrom
• "[T]he mere presence of an incidental future benefit—' some future aspect'—may not warrant capitalization"
